articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on November 13, 2026, targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.
These actions aim to disrupt the financial networks supporting illicit drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally, reinforcing international efforts to combat these threats.
Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, and the implications of these actions, are available on the Treasury website.

articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Designation List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an update to its Iran designation list on November 9, 2026.
This update reflects ongoing efforts to address Iran's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism.
The specific changes to the designation list and their implications for individuals and entities engaging with Iran are detailed in the official announcement.

articles.headline: New Iran-Related Designations Announced by OFAC
body: OFAC announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026, as part of its continued pressure campaign against the Iranian regime.
These designations target specific individuals and entities deemed to be supporting Iran's illicit activities, including its nuclear program and regional destabilization.
The Treasury Department's action underscores its commitment to preventing Iran from acquiring resources that could be used to fund its malign activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Issues Cuba Designations and Determination
body: On November 5, 2026, OFAC announced new designations targeting cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new designations related to Cuba.
The actions against cyber actors and criminal organizations aim to disrupt their financial infrastructure and prevent them from engaging in malicious activities.
Additionally, a Cuba-related determination was published, further clarifying U.S. policy towards the island nation.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, Issues Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing listings.
An Iran-related OFAC Alert was also issued to provide guidance on potential risks and compliance obligations.
Furthermore, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question were published, impacting operations in Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: On October 29, 2026, OFAC issued an amended Iran-related General License.
This amendment provides updated guidance and authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran, potentially impacting various sectors.
Entities engaged in activities related to Iran should review the amended license to ensure compliance with the latest regulations.

The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to addressing threats to international peace and security.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking and Rejecting Transactions and Filing Reports

Compliance professionals should review the revised FAQs to ensure their procedures align with the latest requirements.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, Issues New GLs and Amended FAQs

articles.headline: Drought Conditions Worsen in Central America's Dry Corridor
body: Farming families in Central America's Dry Corridor, stretching across parts of Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador, and Nicaragua, are facing worsening drought conditions.
Over seven million people in this region lack guaranteed access to food, and failed maize or bean harvests are forcing many to seek work elsewhere.

The World Food Programme (WFP) is intensifying its emergency response, providing food and cash assistance to over 470,000 people across Central America, and issuing early warnings for El Niño to help families prepare for drought before it becomes a crisis.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.
This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, easing compliance burdens on the firearms industry while maintaining national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and a license will be required for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, with existing license exceptions for firearms also applicable to suppressors.

articles.headline: Senator Cotton Calls for Addition of Chinese Memory Chipmaker CXMT to Entity List
body: Senator Tom Cotton (R-Arkansas) has sent a letter to Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, requesting that ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT), a Chinese memory chipmaker, be added to the Commerce Department's Entity List.
Cotton argues that CXMT poses a growing risk to American economic prosperity and military superiority due to its ties to the Chinese Communist Party.

The request aims to broadly deny CXMT access to U.S. technologies and technical support, including semiconductor manufacturing equipment and tools for its fabrication facilities, and to explore a prohibition on sales of CXMT products in the American market.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
